note: Exercise form guidelines from authoritative sources (StrongLifts, ACE Fitness, NASM). Used to write precise pose descriptions for avatar image generation. Each entry has start_position and end_position written as visual descriptions suitable for prompting.

exercises.name: Barbell Back Squat
exercises.equipment: Olympic barbell + squat rack/power rack with J-hooks set just below shoulder height; optional lifting belt. Bar loaded with collars.
exercises.primary_muscles: Quadriceps and gluteus maximus (prime movers); hamstrings, adductors, erector spinae/spinal stabilizers, abdominals, calves and upper-back isometric stabilizers.
exercises.start_position: Standing fully erect with the bar racked across the upper back. FEET: heels directly under the shoulder joints (shoulder-width, NOT hip-width), toes turned out approximately 30 degrees, whole foot flat on the floor with heels, forefoot and toes all loaded. BAR: centered on the back (equal knurl rings showing each side) and in a vertical line directly over the MIDFOOT. Low-bar version: bar across the scapular spine, in the shelf between the traps and the rear deltoids. High-bar version: bar on top of the traps at the base of the neck. Never on the bony cervical vertebrae. HANDS: just outside the shoulders. ELBOWS: pointed down and BEHIND the torso at the top — neither vertical/under the bar nor flared horizontally out to the sides. TORSO: vertical, chest raised, upper back arched, shoulder blades squeezed together to create the muscular shelf the bar rests on. SPINE: natural standing lordotic arch, neither rounded nor over-arched. JOINT ANGLES: hips locked ~180 degrees, knees locked ~180 degrees, ankles neutral ~90 degrees, shins vertical. HEAD: in line with the torso, neck neutral, gaze straight ahead and slightly down at the floor-wall junction — not up at the ceiling, not down at the feet.
exercises.end_position: Bottom of the rep. DEPTH: the hip crease is LOWER than the top of the kneecaps — hips below knees, past parallel. Thighs-parallel-to-floor is not deep enough; full ass-to-grass (butt near ankles) is too deep and tends to round the lumbar spine. JOINT ANGLES: knee flexed to roughly 60-70 degrees of included angle (deep flexion), hip included angle roughly 50-60 degrees between femur and torso, ankle dorsiflexed roughly 20-25 degrees so the SHINS ARE INCLINED FORWARD (shins must not be vertical). TORSO: leaning forward — about 40-50 degrees from vertical for a low-bar squat, a more upright 25-30 degrees from vertical for high-bar; exact angle varies with build and bar position. KNEES: pushed out to the sides, tracking directly over and slightly past the toes, thighs in line with the 30-degree foot splay. BAR: still in the same vertical line over the midfoot — it has not drifted toward the toes or the heels. BACK: same natural arch as at the top, completely unchanged. ELBOWS: now in line with the torso rather than behind it. HEAD: still in line with the torso, gaze unchanged. Hips then rise straight up while the back angle is maintained, knees stay pushed out, chest stays up, and hips and knees lock together at the top.
exercises.hand_grip_detail: Pronated grip with the bar behind the neck. Width is MEDIUM — hands just outside the shoulders, narrower than a bench press grip; roughly 1.2-1.3x shoulder width. Thumbs may be fully wrapped around the bar (full grip) or left on top of the bar (thumbless), but the hands only SQUEEZE the bar hard for tension — they carry none of the load. Wrists bend slightly backward in the low-bar position; the wrist must stay relatively straight rather than collapsing back, and the bar is supported by the upper back shelf, never held up by the hands. Hands placed symmetrically, equal distance from the center knurl.
exercises.body_alignment_cues: Lumbar spine holds its natural inward arch from first rep to last — this is the single thing that must never change shape. Upper back actively arched and shoulder blades pinched to build the bar shelf; elbows driven down and back to engage the lats, which stiffens the torso. Hips and knees bend AT THE SAME TIME — the hips travel back and down while the knees push out. This is a combined hip hinge and knee bend, not one or the other. Whole foot stays flat and planted: imagine gripping the floor and screwing the feet outward to stop the knees caving. Bar travels in a straight vertical line over the midfoot, which is the balance point. WHAT MOVES: hips, knees and ankles; the torso rotates about the hips as a single rigid segment. WHAT STAYS STILL: the spine's shape, the position of the bar on the back, the hands, the wrists, the head's alignment with the torso, and the feet. Descent is controlled; ascent is as fast as form allows. Breath is taken in at the top and held through the descent and bottom, exhaled at the top.
common_form_mistakes: Knees caving inward (valgus) on the way up — thighs no longer in line with the feet, which twists the knee joints
Heels rising off the floor and weight shifting onto the toes, usually from too narrow a stance or the bar drifting forward
Lower back rounding at the bottom ('butt wink'), typically from squatting too deep or too narrow
Excessive forward lean — the hips rise faster than the chest out of the bottom and the torso collapses toward horizontal
Not reaching depth: stopping at or above thighs-parallel instead of getting the hip crease below the top of the knee
Shins staying vertical at the bottom, which forces more forward lean and loads the lower back
Looking up at the ceiling or down at the feet instead of keeping the head in line with the torso — looking down pulls the lifter forward
Bar placed on the bony base of the neck instead of on the upper-back muscle shelf, causing neck pain
Chest collapsing and upper back rounding so the bar rolls up toward the neck
Stance too narrow, so the torso blocks the legs and full depth becomes impossible
Knees shooting forward while the hips fail to travel back
Descending too fast and losing position at the bottom

exercises.name: Conventional Barbell Deadlift
exercises.equipment: Olympic barbell loaded with plates resting on the floor; flat-soled shoes or bare feet. Optional lifting belt and chalk. No rack needed.
exercises.primary_muscles: Gluteus maximus, hamstrings and erector spinae (prime movers); quadriceps for the initial break from the floor, plus lats, traps, rhomboids, forearm flexors/grip, abdominals and adductors. ACE classifies it as a full-body/integrated lift.
exercises.start_position: Crouched over the bar, which is still on the floor. FEET: heels about HIP-WIDTH apart — narrower than the squat stance — toes turned out about 15 degrees, whole foot flat. BAR: positioned over the MIDFOOT so that looking down the bar visually cuts each foot in half; this leaves the bar roughly one inch in front of the shins before the knees bend, and the shins come forward to lightly touch the bar at the bottom of the setup. HANDS: just outside the shins, about shoulder-width, arms hanging straight. ARMS: completely straight and locked at the elbow, vertical when viewed from the front, slightly inclined when viewed from the side. SHOULDERS: the shoulder BLADES sit directly above the bar and above the midfoot, which places the shoulder JOINTS slightly in front of the bar from a side view. HIPS: higher than the knees but well below the shoulders — the setup looks like a half squat, not a deep squat and not a stiff-leg hinge. Exact hip height is dictated by limb proportions. JOINT ANGLES: knees flexed to roughly 130-145 degrees, hip included angle roughly 90-110 degrees, torso inclined roughly 20-45 degrees above horizontal depending on build, shins slightly inclined forward. BACK: lower back NEUTRAL with its normal inward curve, chest lifted, upper back tight. HEAD: neck in line with the rest of the spine, gaze fixed on a point on the floor a few feet in front — not up at the mirror, not down at the feet.
exercises.end_position: Full lockout, standing tall. Hips and knees both fully straightened to 180 degrees but NOT hyperextended. Torso vertical, lower back holding its natural arch. Bar resting against the upper thighs at the hip crease, arms hanging straight and perfectly vertical from the shoulders. Shoulders pulled back and down — not shrugged up toward the ears, and the torso does NOT lean back behind vertical. Chest up, head neutral and in line with the torso, gaze forward. Feet unchanged: same hip-width stance, toes still out 15 degrees, whole foot flat. The bar has travelled in a straight vertical line from over the midfoot to the hip crease. On the way down the hips are pushed back first, the bar slides down the thighs, and the knees only bend once the bar passes them, so the bar descends in the same vertical line.
exercises.hand_grip_detail: The NARROWEST grip of the barbell lifts — hands just outside the shins, roughly shoulder-width (the same width as the overhead press), which shortens the range of motion and makes bracing easier. DOUBLE OVERHAND (both palms facing the lifter, pronated) with the thumbs fully wrapped around the bar; switch to a MIXED grip (one palm facing back, one facing forward) only once double overhand fails on heavy weight. Never thumbless. The bar is held LOW in the hand, closer to the base of the fingers than the mid-palm, so the palm skin does not fold and tear. Arms remain dead straight the whole rep — they are cables, not levers. ACE's version of the lift specifies the over-under (mixed) grip from the start.
exercises.body_alignment_cues: Lower back is neutral throughout: the normal inward curve, with no rounding and no exaggerated arch. Hips and shoulders must rise AT THE SAME RATE — if the hips shoot up first, the legs are taken out of the lift and the whole load lands on the back. Chest stays lifted and the lats are engaged to keep the bar pinned close to the body, dragging lightly up the shins and thighs. Knees are pushed out to the sides during the setup so the arms clear them. Neck stays in line with the spine — the head does not crane up at lockout. WHAT MOVES: hips and knees extending together, the torso rotating up about the hips as one rigid segment. WHAT STAYS STILL: the spine's shape, the straight arms, the elbows, the grip, the head's alignment with the torso, and the feet, which stay flat and planted. The bar never leaves the vertical line over the midfoot. ACE's cue: when it is done correctly the glutes and hamstrings do the work, NOT the lower back. Each rep is reset on the floor rather than bounced.
common_form_mistakes: Rounded lower back under load, which compresses the spinal discs from the front
Hyper-extending/over-arching the lower back at lockout, compressing the discs from the back
Letting the bar drift forward away from the shins, which lengthens the bar path and spikes back stress
Hips rising before the chest, which removes the legs from the lift and dumps the load on the back
Setting up with the hips too high (like a stiff-leg deadlift) or too low (like a squat) — a squat-style setup pushes the knees into the bar
Bending the elbows during the pull, which risks a biceps tear on heavy weights
Standing too far from the bar so the bar starts over the toes rather than the midfoot
Leaning back at the top and shrugging the shoulders instead of simply standing tall
Jerking the bar off the floor instead of pulling the slack out and applying force smoothly
Failing to push the hips back first on the descent, so the knees block the bar's vertical path
Bouncing the bar off the floor between reps, using the rebound instead of the muscles
Craning the neck up to look in the mirror, which breaks cervical alignment

exercises.name: Flat Barbell Bench Press
exercises.equipment: Olympic barbell with collars, flat bench with uprights inside a power rack with safety pins/arms set below chest height. A spotter is strongly recommended.
exercises.primary_muscles: Pectoralis major (sternal and clavicular heads) as prime mover; anterior deltoid and triceps brachii as major contributors; serratus anterior, biceps and forearm as stabilizers, with lats, glutes and legs providing isometric support and leg drive.
exercises.start_position: Lying supine on the bench with the bar held at arm's length above the shoulders, elbows locked, having just been unracked. FIVE POINTS OF CONTACT: (1) head resting lightly on the bench, (2) upper back and shoulder blades pressed into the bench, (3) buttocks on the bench, (4) and (5) both feet flat on the floor. FEET: flat, heels down, positioned under or slightly behind the knees, about shoulder-width apart heel to heel, toes turned out roughly 30 degrees. SHOULDER BLADES: pinched together and pulled back and DOWN into the bench, which is what creates a stable pressing platform. BACK: natural lumbar arch — about a hand's thickness of gap under the lower back — created by pushing the chest UP, not by cranking the lower spine. HEAD: eyes positioned directly under the bar at setup so the unrack path is short; neck neutral, touching the bench only lightly. BAR AND ARMS: bar directly above the shoulder joints, arms vertical, elbows fully extended to ~180 degrees, wrists stacked straight over the elbows.
exercises.end_position: Bottom of the rep, bar touching the chest. TOUCH POINT: mid-chest — the middle of the breastbone, between the nipple line and the bottom of the sternum. Same spot every single rep. ELBOWS: tucked to roughly 75 degrees from the torso (NOT flared to 90 degrees, and not pinned against the ribs), and positioned directly UNDER the bar. FOREARMS: vertical to the floor when viewed from BOTH the side and the front; a straight line runs from the bar through the wrist to the elbow. ELBOW ANGLE: roughly 45-60 degrees of flexion, varying with grip width and torso depth. Shoulder blades still pinched and depressed, chest still pushed up, lumbar arch unchanged, buttocks still on the bench, both feet still flat. The bar makes brief contact — touch and go, no pause-bounce, no half reps. BAR PATH: not vertical. The bar travels a shallow diagonal/J-curve, moving down and slightly forward from above the shoulders to the mid-chest, then back up and slightly BACK so it finishes over the shoulder joints with the elbows locked.
exercises.hand_grip_detail: Pronated (palms facing the feet). Width is MEDIUM: pinky fingers just inside the bar's ring marks, which works out to roughly 1.5x shoulder width for most lifters; pointer fingers ON the rings (81 cm between index fingers) is the widest competition-legal grip. ACE describes it more conservatively as slightly wider than shoulder width. THUMBS FULLY WRAPPED around the bar — never the thumbless 'suicide' grip, which lets the bar slide onto the chest or throat. The bar sits LOW in the hand, in the heel/base of the palm close to the wrist, NOT high in the fingers, so the wrist stays straight instead of cocked back. Rotate the hands inward before closing the grip ('bulldog grip') so the bar settles into the palm heel. Hands equidistant from the center knurl.
exercises.body_alignment_cues: The shoulder blades are retracted and depressed and HOLD that position for the whole set — if they come loose the shoulder rolls forward and is exposed. Chest stays high and proud; the lumbar arch is natural and unchanging. The glutes stay squeezed and on the bench while the heels drive into the floor (leg drive), which pushes the chest slightly higher and helps move the bar up and back off the chest. Wrists stay neutral and stacked over the elbows. Head stays neutral on the bench and does not turn to look for the uprights. WHAT MOVES: the shoulders and elbows only. WHAT STAYS STILL: the shoulder blades, the back arch, the buttocks, both feet, the head, the wrists and the grip. Elbows are locked at the top of every rep.
common_form_mistakes: Flaring the elbows out to 90 degrees from the torso, which drives shoulder impingement — tuck to about 75 degrees
Using a thumbless grip, which lets the bar slip off the hands onto the chest or neck
Bending the wrists backward because the bar is held high in the palm, causing wrist pain and leaking force
Letting the shoulder blades unpinch and the chest flatten, which forces the bar to touch too low and exposes the shoulder joint
Touching the bar far too low on the abdomen, needlessly lengthening the range of motion
Driving the bar straight up off the chest instead of up and slightly back, which overloads the shoulders
Lifting the buttocks off the bench to shorten the range of motion
Putting the feet up on the bench or in the air, losing stability and leg drive
Not locking the elbows at the top, so the rep is incomplete and control is poor
Bouncing the bar off the chest or stopping short of the chest (half reps)
Benching without safety pins, straps or a spotter
Elbows still pointing forward with the shoulders externally rotated at lockout, which blocks a clean finish

exercises.name: Standing Barbell Overhead Press (Shoulder Press)
exercises.equipment: Olympic barbell with collars; power rack with J-hooks set at roughly upper-chest/clavicle height to unrack from. Performed standing, with no bench and no leg drive.
exercises.primary_muscles: Anterior and lateral deltoids (prime movers) and triceps brachii; upper trapezius and serratus anterior for scapular upward rotation; plus a large isometric contribution from the erector spinae, abdominals, glutes and quadriceps, which stabilize the whole body under an overhead load.
exercises.start_position: Standing erect with the bar resting on the front of the shoulders. FEET: heels about HIP-WIDTH apart, flat on the floor, toes turned slightly out (roughly 15 degrees). BAR: resting across the front deltoids, just below the collarbones — supported by the shoulders, not held up by the arms. HANDS: just outside the shoulders — a NARROW grip, narrower than the bench press grip. ELBOWS: almost directly UNDER the bar when viewed from the side, and angled roughly 45 degrees in toward the midline when viewed from the front. FOREARMS: vertical to the floor from both the side and front views. Upper arms are NOT horizontal (that would be a front-squat rack position). WRISTS: almost straight with the knuckles rotated back about 75 degrees; bar in the base of the palm. TORSO: chest lifted by arching the upper back, lower back neutral, hips pushed slightly forward so the torso leans back a small amount at the start to clear the chin. HIPS AND KNEES: fully locked straight — no dip, no bend. HEAD: neutral, gaze fixed on a point on the wall straight ahead; not tilted up.
exercises.end_position: Full lockout overhead. Bar in a vertical line directly above the shoulder joints AND above the midfoot — the balance point. Elbows locked straight, arms vertical, upper arms beside the ears. SHOULDERS SHRUGGED up toward the ceiling at the very top to bring the traps in and clear the rotator cuff. The torso has moved FORWARD under the bar so the whole body forms a straight vertical line from midfoot through hips, shoulders and bar — the slight lean-back from the start has been removed, and there is no backward lean at lockout. Lower back neutral, no exaggerated arch. Head neutral: on the way up it travels BACK a few inches to let the bar pass the face, then comes forward under the bar at lockout. Hips and knees still locked. Gaze forward. BAR PATH: a straight vertical line over the midfoot, achieved by moving the head and then the torso around the bar rather than by swinging the bar around the head.
exercises.hand_grip_detail: Pronated. NARROW width — hands just outside the shoulders, roughly the same width as a deadlift grip and clearly narrower than a bench press grip, so that the forearms can be vertical. Thumbs fully WRAPPED around the bar (a thumbless grip can let the bar slip back onto the head). Bar held LOW in the hand, in the base of the palm close to the wrist, using the inward-rotated 'bulldog' hand placement, so the wrist stays nearly straight with the knuckles back about 75 degrees rather than collapsing into full extension. ACE's variant notes gripping about shoulder-width with the palms facing the ceiling and the elbows pointing straight ahead when the bar is racked on the shoulders.
exercises.body_alignment_cues: Forearms vertical from every angle is the master cue for grip width and elbow position. Lower back stays NEUTRAL — the press is driven by the shoulders and triceps, not by leaning back and turning it into an incline press. Upper back is arched to lift the chest; abs, glutes and quads are braced hard isometrically to hold the body rigid under an overhead load. Hips and knees stay LOCKED from start to finish — any knee bend turns it into a push press. The head is the only thing that gets out of the way: it moves back as the bar clears the face, then forward under the bar at lockout. Shrug the traps at the top. WHAT MOVES: shoulders and elbows, plus a small backward-then-forward shift of the head and torso around a fixed vertical bar path. WHAT STAYS STILL: the feet, the knees, the hips, the grip, the wrists and the shape of the lower back.
common_form_mistakes: Bending the knees to launch the bar — that is a push press, not a strict overhead press
Using a bench-press-width grip, which inclines the forearms and robs the press of leverage
Flaring the elbows out to the sides instead of keeping them about 45 degrees in and under the bar
Letting the wrists bend fully backward, which hurts and leaks force
Over-arching the lower back and leaning back to turn the press into a standing incline press
Tilting the head up to watch the bar, which causes neck strain and encourages the lean-back
Using a thumbless grip, so the bar can slip back toward the head
Not locking the elbows at the top, so the rep is short and poorly controlled
Pressing the bar forward in an arc around the head instead of straight up over the midfoot
Failing to shrug the shoulders at lockout, leaving the rotator cuff in an impingement-prone position
Letting the heels rise or the toes lift as balance shifts
Arms forward of the body at lockout rather than stacked over the shoulders and midfoot

exercises.name: Barbell Bent-Over Row
exercises.equipment: Olympic barbell loaded on the floor; chalk optional. No rack, no bench — the bar is deadlifted into position and each rep starts from the floor.
exercises.primary_muscles: Latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, middle and lower trapezius, posterior deltoid and teres major (prime movers); biceps brachii, brachialis and forearm flexors assist; erector spinae, glutes and hamstrings work isometrically to hold the bent-over torso position. ACE lists the targets as arms, back and shoulders.
exercises.start_position: Bent over the bar, which rests on the floor. FEET: MEDIUM stance — wider than the deadlift stance but narrower than the squat stance; toes turned out about 30 degrees, pointed the same direction as the knees, whole foot flat. BAR: over the MIDFOOT, the balance point. TORSO: HORIZONTAL, parallel to the floor — this is the defining geometry of the lift. HIPS: set HIGH, higher than in a deadlift setup, so the bar has room to travel. KNEES: unlocked and slightly bent, but held BACK so the bar's vertical path cannot hit them; knees pushed out to the sides. BACK: lower back neutral with the same natural arch as standing; chest raised toward the ceiling. ARMS: hanging straight down, perfectly vertical, elbows fully extended, shoulder blades allowed to spread slightly. HANDS: double overhand, grip width between a deadlift and a bench press. HEAD: neutral, in line with the rest of the spine so there is a straight line from the head through the hips; gaze down and slightly forward — not up at the mirror, not straight down at the feet.
exercises.end_position: Top of the pull. The bar has travelled in a straight VERTICAL line from over the midfoot up to touch the LOWER CHEST / bottom of the sternum. ELBOWS: pulled back BEHIND the torso, tucked roughly 75 degrees in from the torso rather than flared out at 90 degrees; elbow flexion roughly 45-60 degrees. Shoulder blades retracted and squeezed together at the top. TORSO: still essentially horizontal — it may rise no more than about 15 degrees above its starting angle; it must not swing up toward vertical. HIPS AND KNEES: unchanged from the start position. Wrists straight, forearms in line with the pull, lower back still neutral, head still in line with the spine. The bar is then lowered under control all the way back to the floor and RESET between reps, rather than being held hovering in the air.
exercises.hand_grip_detail: DOUBLE OVERHAND (both palms facing down/back, pronated) — not a mixed grip. Width is intermediate: narrower than a bench press grip but wider than a deadlift grip, roughly shoulder width to slightly outside the shoulders, so the arms hang vertically from the shoulders and the forearms stay in line with the pull. Thumbs fully WRAPPED around the bar; not thumbless. The bar is held LOW in the hands, close to the base of the fingers rather than the mid-palm, which prevents skin folding and calluses. Wrists stay STRAIGHT and in line with the forearm the whole rep — letting them bend backward produces the short-levered 'T-Rex row'. ACE's cue for the same position: wrists, elbows and shoulders lined up in a straight line.
exercises.body_alignment_cues: The horizontal torso is the whole point: set it parallel to the floor and keep it there, allowing at most 15 degrees of rise. Lower back stays neutral with its natural standing arch; chest stays raised. Hips are high and knees are back, so the bar's vertical path is clear. Head stays in line with the spine, giving one straight line from skull to hips. The pull comes from the elbows driving back past the torso and the shoulder blades squeezing together — not from the biceps and not from standing up. WHAT MOVES: the shoulders and elbows only, and the bar in a strictly vertical line between the midfoot and the lower chest. WHAT STAYS STILL: the torso angle, the hips, the knees, the feet, the shape of the lower back, the head alignment and the wrists. Reset the bar on the floor between reps so the back is not loaded in the bent-over position for the whole set.
common_form_mistakes: Rounding the lower back while bent over, which compresses the spinal discs under load
Letting the torso swing up more than about 15 degrees, which shifts the work to the hips and turns the lift into a deadlift
Dropping the chest down to meet the bar instead of pulling the bar up to the chest, cutting the range of motion
Straightening the knees to initiate the pull — the legs should not generate the movement
Setting the hips too low, which puts the knees in the bar's path
Keeping the bar hovering in the air between reps, which fatigues the back and leads to rounding
Bending the wrists backward ('T-Rex rows') instead of keeping them straight and in line with the forearms
Elbows drifting too far forward, or flaring out to 90 degrees, instead of tucking about 75 degrees and travelling behind the torso
Pulling the bar to the belly or the hips rather than to the lower chest/sternum
Jerking and using momentum rather than a controlled vertical pull
Looking up at the mirror, which breaks the head-to-hip line
Bar starting over the toes rather than over the midfoot, so the pull is not vertical

exercises.name: Pull-Up
exercises.equipment: Fixed horizontal pull-up bar mounted overhead, high enough for a full dead hang with the feet clear of the floor. Bodyweight only; optional resistance band or box for assistance, or a dip belt for added load. A step or box is used to reach the bar.
exercises.primary_muscles: Latissimus dorsi and rhomboids as prime movers; secondary contribution from the biceps brachii, brachialis, middle trapezius, posterior deltoid, teres major and the core stabilizers. ACE's chin-up version shifts more load onto the biceps brachii, brachialis and brachioradialis.
exercises.start_position: Full dead hang from the bar. HANDS: slightly WIDER than shoulder-width apart, pronated — palms facing away from the body — with the thumbs wrapped around the bar. ARMS: fully extended overhead, elbows at roughly 180 degrees. SHOULDER BLADES: DEPRESSED and 'packed' — actively pulled down the back and away from the ears before the pull begins, not left passively shrugged up around the neck. TORSO: hanging vertically, spine long and neutral, chest lifted, abdominals braced; no sag in the lower back. LEGS: squeezed together and still, either straight and hanging directly below the body or with the knees bent and the ANKLES CROSSED behind, which kills the swing. HEAD: neutral, neck in line with the spine, gaze forward or slightly up at the bar — not craned. The whole body hangs as one rigid vertical line, motionless before the first rep.
exercises.end_position: Top of the rep. The CHIN clears the top of the bar, or the upper chest approaches the bar. ELBOWS: driven DOWNWARD and back, pulled past the rib cage; elbow flexion roughly 40-60 degrees of included angle. SHOULDER BLADES: fully retracted and depressed — squeezed together and down — with the chest lifted toward the bar. TORSO: still essentially vertical, leaning back only very slightly; no large arch, no hip pike, no kipping swing. LEGS: still together and still crossed/quiet, in the same place relative to the torso as at the start. Head neutral — the chin clears the bar because the BODY rose, not because the neck craned forward. Hold the top position for a brief pause, then lower with control all the way back to the full dead hang with the arms straight and the shoulder blades depressed again, maintaining tension in the back throughout and never dropping or free-falling.
exercises.hand_grip_detail: Pronated (overhand) grip for a true pull-up: palms facing away from the lifter, hands slightly wider than shoulder-width — roughly 1.2-1.5x shoulder width. Thumbs wrapped around the bar for security. A wider grip biases the latissimus dorsi; a narrower grip brings in more biceps. The hands stay FIXED on the bar — no regripping or shifting mid-rep. ACE's technique series prefers the SUPINATED chin-up grip (palms facing the lifter, about shoulder-width), on the grounds that supination externally rotates the shoulder and aligns the forearm bones naturally, which reduces impingement risk; the pull-up's pronated grip is the harder, more lat-dominant version of the same movement.
exercises.body_alignment_cues: Set the scapulae FIRST: before the elbows bend at all, pull the shoulder blades down and together — 'put them in your back pocket.' Then pull by driving the elbows down and back past the rib cage, thinking of lifting the CHEST to the bar rather than hauling with the arms. Spine stays long and stiff with the abs braced, so the body moves as one rigid unit. Legs squeezed together with the ankles crossed to prevent the body from swinging; the lower body should look frozen for the whole rep. WHAT MOVES: the shoulders and elbows, and the body translating vertically up and down. WHAT STAYS STILL: the hands on the bar, the spine's shape, the head's alignment with the spine, and the legs relative to the torso. Both directions are controlled — the lowering phase is as deliberate as the pull, with the back staying under tension rather than relaxing into the bottom.
common_form_mistakes: Using momentum or kipping — swinging the hips and legs to throw the body up on what should be a strict-strength rep
Pulling primarily with the arms and biceps instead of initiating with the back and driving the elbows down
Incomplete range of motion: starting from a half-bent arm instead of a full dead hang, or stopping before the chin clears the bar
Jumping up to the top and then only lowering halfway before dropping off
Uncontrolled, jerky or free-fall lowering, which loses the eccentric work and strains the shoulder
Failing to depress and pack the shoulder blades at the bottom, hanging passively with the shoulders shrugged up around the ears
Craning the neck forward to get the chin over the bar instead of raising the body
Losing core bracing so the lower back arches and the hips pike or sway
Letting the legs swing, which also makes the grip harder to hold and raises injury risk
Flaring the elbows wide out to the sides instead of driving them down and back past the ribs
Letting the shoulders roll forward at the top rather than squeezing the blades back and down
Shortening the hang by bending the knees up toward the chest to shorten the pull

exercises.name: Dumbbell Bicep Curl (standing, both arms)
exercises.equipment: Two dumbbells (bench optional for the seated variation)
exercises.primary_muscles: Biceps brachii (primary); brachialis and brachioradialis assist; forearm flexors and anterior deltoid stabilize
exercises.start_position: Standing tall, feet flat and hip-width apart (about 15-25 cm between the insteps), toes pointing straight forward, knees soft (about 5-10 degrees of flexion, not locked). Pelvis neutral, ribcage stacked over pelvis, natural small lumbar arch. Dumbbells hang at arm's length beside the thighs, the dumbbell handles roughly level with the mid-thigh and about 2-5 cm clear of the leg. Elbows fully extended (about 170-180 degrees), upper arms vertical and pinned alongside the ribs so the elbow points straight back at the floor-wall line. Shoulders depressed and retracted (scapulae pulled down and back), so the collarbones look wide and the traps look long, not bunched. Wrists neutral and straight, forearms supinated so palms face forward. Head stacked over the shoulders, chin level, gaze straight ahead at eye level. In the seated version the head, upper back and glutes all stay in contact with the backrest and both feet are planted flat on the floor.
exercises.end_position: Elbows flexed to roughly 40-55 degrees of remaining angle (dumbbells finishing at upper-chest/front-of-shoulder height, about 10-15 cm in front of the collarbone). The upper arm is still vertical: the elbow has NOT travelled forward, so the point of the elbow stays directly under the shoulder joint, in the same spot it occupied at the start. Forearm now angles up and slightly inward, palms facing the chest/ceiling, wrists still straight and in line with the forearm (no curling of the knuckles toward the biceps). Torso is identical to the start - no lean back, no hip thrust, lumbar arch unchanged. Shoulders still down and back, traps quiet. Knees and feet unchanged. Gaze still level and forward. The rep path is a tight arc in a single plane beside the torso: nothing else in the body moves between the two frames, which makes the elbow the only animated joint (plus a very slight forearm supination if animating the rotating variation).
exercises.hand_grip_detail: Closed, supinated grip: palms facing forward at the start, thumbs wrapped fully around the handle opposite the fingers (not a thumbless grip). Hands set at hip-width/shoulder-width, directly under the shoulder joints, with the handle sitting across the middle of the palm at the base of the fingers so the dumbbell is centred - no loading toward the pinky or index side. Wrist stays in line with the forearm the whole time; the knuckles stay flat, never flexed toward the forearm.
exercises.body_alignment_cues: Spine neutral with its natural lumbar curve; torso braced by contracting the abdominals so the ribcage cannot flare. Scapulae depressed and retracted and HELD there for every rep - no shrug at the top. Upper arms are the fixed segment: they stay glued to the sides of the torso and the elbows stay under the shoulders, so only the forearms move. Hips and knees are static - no hip hinge, no rocking, no knee dip to generate momentum. Head follows the spine, gaze horizontal.
common_form_mistakes: Rocking the torso or thrusting the hips to swing the weight up (ACE: do not rock for momentum; if the back starts to arch, lower the weight)
Arching the lower back and leaning the shoulders behind the hips at the top
Letting the elbows drift forward so the dumbbells travel up and in and the front delts take over
Shrugging the shoulders - losing scapular depression at the top of the curl
Flexing the wrists (curling the knuckles toward the biceps), which shifts load to the forearm and stresses the elbow
Swinging the arm away from the body instead of keeping the upper arm against the ribs
Dropping the weight on the way down instead of lowering under control
In the seated version, letting the head, upper back or glutes come off the bench, or lifting the feet off the floor

exercises.name: Tricep Pushdown (cable, bar or rope attachment)
exercises.equipment: Cable machine with the pulley set above head height, straight/angled bar or rope attachment
exercises.primary_muscles: Triceps brachii (all three heads; the long head is loaded less than in overhead variations). Core, lats and scapular stabilizers hold position
exercises.start_position: Standing facing the cable stack, roughly one forearm's length (about 25-40 cm) back from the weight stack so the cable hangs just clear of the chest. Feet either hip-width apart and square, or in a short staggered stance (one foot about half a stride forward) for a stable base; weight even through both feet, knees slightly bent. Torso vertical and perpendicular to the floor - essentially no forward lean - with the natural lumbar arch preserved and the abdominals braced. Shoulders depressed and retracted and held there. Upper arms vertical and pinned to the sides so the elbows sit level with the midpoint of the trunk, roughly beside the lower ribs. Elbows flexed to about 90 degrees (can start slightly higher, around 100-110 degrees, with the hands near upper-chest height) so the forearms angle up toward the pulley. Wrists neutral and straight. Head in line with the spine, chin level, gaze straight ahead or very slightly down at the hands - never craning down at the floor.
exercises.end_position: Elbows extended to full (but not forcibly locked) extension, roughly 170-180 degrees, so the arms form one straight line from shoulder to knuckles beside the thighs. Hands finish at about hip or upper-thigh height, 5-15 cm in front of the thighs. Upper arms have NOT moved: the elbows are still beside the lower ribs at the trunk's midpoint, the same spot as at the start. Torso still vertical - no hinge forward, no lean over the bar, no shoulder roll forward. Shoulders still down and back; wrists still straight and in line with the forearms. With a rope the hands also separate and rotate slightly so the palms turn toward each other/down and the rope ends finish just outside the thighs; with a straight bar the hands stay pronated and the bar stays level. Brief pause at full extension, then the forearms swing back up along the same arc until the elbows reach about 90-110 degrees and the hands are back near the upper chest - stopping before the elbows drift forward of the trunk line. Only the elbow joint animates; everything above and below it is a held pose.
exercises.hand_grip_detail: Full closed grip with the thumbs clasped around the handle, hands set about shoulder-width or slightly narrower (roughly 15-30 cm apart on a straight bar) and symmetrical about the body's midline. Straight/angled bar: overhand (pronated) grip, palms facing down/away, bar resting across the base of the fingers into the mid-palm, knuckles in line with the forearm. Rope: neutral grip, palms facing each other, each hand gripping near the end of the rope with the thumbs on top and the fingers wrapped, the rope ends resting against the little-finger side of the hands.
exercises.body_alignment_cues: Spine neutral with a maintained natural lumbar arch; abdominals braced to stop the ribcage and pelvis moving. Torso stays vertically aligned with the floor for the whole rep. Scapulae depressed and retracted throughout. The upper arms are the anchored segment - they stay firmly by the sides with the elbows at the trunk's midpoint - and the forearms are the only moving segment. Hips and knees stay still: no bob, no hip hinge to drive the bar down. Head neutral, gaze forward.
common_form_mistakes: Letting the elbows travel forward of the trunk's midline, which recruits the lats and removes load from the triceps (ACE's main cue for this lift)
Leaning the torso forward over the bar and using bodyweight to push the handle down
Standing too far from the stack, which pulls the arms forward and forces the lean
Flaring the elbows out away from the ribs instead of keeping the upper arms pinned
Letting the shoulders roll forward and up - losing scapular depression and retraction
Breaking the wrists (flexing or extending) instead of keeping them neutral
Slamming into a hard elbow lock-out rather than finishing at full extension without locking
Shortening the range at the top by letting the hands rise past the upper chest with the elbows flying forward, or cutting it short and never reaching extension
Bouncing the knees or hips to help the weight down

exercises.name: Dumbbell Lateral Raise
exercises.primary_muscles: Middle (lateral) deltoid (primary); anterior deltoid and supraspinatus assist; upper traps and scapular stabilizers hold the shoulder girdle down
exercises.start_position: Standing with the dumbbells alongside the thighs. Feet either slightly wider than hip-width (about 25-35 cm apart, toes forward) or in a split stance for extra balance; knees slightly bent, weight even through both feet. Torso erect and vertical, abdominals and core braced ('bracing'), ribcage stacked over the pelvis, natural lumbar curve. Scapulae depressed and retracted - shoulders pulled down and back - and held there. Arms hang down beside the thighs with the elbows either fully extended or holding a slight bend (roughly 10-20 degrees), and the dumbbells about 5-10 cm clear of the outer thighs. Neutral grip: palms facing in toward the body. Wrists straight. Head aligned with the spine, chin level, gaze straight ahead.
exercises.end_position: Arms raised out to the sides until they reach shoulder height and are approximately parallel with the floor - the body makes a wide T, with the shoulder-to-hand line horizontal and the dumbbells roughly level with the top of the shoulders. Elbow angle is unchanged from the start (still extended or holding that same slight 10-20 degree bend), and the elbows and upper arms stay slightly AHEAD of the forearms and dumbbells, so the arms sit a few degrees forward of the frontal plane rather than straight out to the sides. As the arms pass about 60-70 degrees of elevation they rotate slightly upward so the front edge of each dumbbell points slightly up (thumb side a touch higher than the little-finger side); the hands do not pour forward into a thumbs-down position. Wrists stay neutral and in line with the forearms - no breaking upward at the top. Torso still erect and vertical with no lean back or side-to-side sway; shoulders still depressed, traps not shrugged up toward the ears. Knees and feet unchanged, gaze still level and forward. The return is the same arc reversed, with the arms rotating slightly downward again as they pass back through 60-70 degrees, finishing at the thighs - one clean fan-shaped sweep in which only the shoulder joint animates.
exercises.hand_grip_detail: Closed, neutral grip: thumbs wrapped around the handles with the palms facing the body/thighs at the start. The handle sits across the mid-palm with the dumbbell balanced evenly front to back, hands directly below the shoulder joints and about hip-width apart. Through the raise the grip stays neutral (palms facing down/outward at shoulder height with the thumb side a few degrees high after the slight external rotation at 60-70 degrees). Wrists stay straight and relaxed - no squeezing the handle into wrist extension, no thumbs-pointing-at-the-floor pouring motion.
exercises.body_alignment_cues: Erect, vertical torso braced by the abdominals and core; ribcage down, natural lumbar curve. Scapulae depressed and retracted throughout, with the head aligned with the spine. Slight knee flex and a wide or split foot base to resist swaying. The shoulder joint is the only joint that moves: the elbow angle is fixed and the wrists are fixed, so the whole arm travels as one unit. No hip hinge or torso rock, and no vertical bob of the body to launch the weights. The slight upward arm rotation past 60-70 degrees is what keeps the shoulder out of impingement in this internally rotated pattern.
common_form_mistakes: Using too much weight and swinging/heaving the dumbbells up with hip and knee drive
Shrugging - letting the upper traps lift the shoulders toward the ears and losing scapular depression
Raising the arms above shoulder height so the arms pass parallel with the floor
Keeping the arms strictly out to the sides (or behind the frontal plane) instead of letting the elbows and upper arms stay slightly ahead of the forearms
Omitting the slight upward rotation past 60-70 degrees, or over-rotating into a thumbs-down 'pouring' position, both of which increase shoulder impingement risk
Bending and straightening the elbows during the rep - turning the raise into a swinging curl-like motion
Leaning the torso back or arching the lower back to get the weights up
Letting the wrists break upward so the dumbbells tilt back at the top
Dropping the dumbbells back to the thighs instead of controlling the lowering phase

exercises.name: Dumbbell Shoulder Press (seated overhead press)
exercises.equipment: Two dumbbells and an upright bench with a back support (can also be done standing)
exercises.primary_muscles: Anterior and middle deltoid (primary); triceps brachii and upper traps/serratus assist; core and lats stabilize
exercises.start_position: Seated upright with the back against the bench pad so the head, shoulders and glutes all make contact with the bench; feet planted firmly and flat on the floor, roughly hip- to shoulder-width apart, shins near vertical. Core braced. Dumbbells held at shoulder level with a closed, pronated grip (palms facing forward), hands set at shoulder-width or slightly wider; the dumbbell handles sit roughly level with the top of the shoulders/ears, just outside the line of the shoulders. Elbows flexed to roughly 90 degrees, pointing down and FORWARD (about 30-45 degrees in front of the frontal plane) rather than flared straight out to the sides into a goal-post position. Forearms near vertical under the dumbbells. Wrists neutral - straight, not cocked back under the weight. Scapulae retracted and depressed (pulled down and back) and held. Spine neutral with its natural lumbar curve and no excess arch. Head stacked on the spine against the pad, chin level, gaze straight ahead.
exercises.end_position: Dumbbells pressed overhead in unison until the elbows are fully extended (about 170-180 degrees), with the dumbbells finishing directly above the shoulder joints, roughly over the ears or a touch behind the forehead line - not out in front of the face. The arms are near vertical, upper arms close to in line with the torso, and the hands may travel slightly inward so the dumbbells end up nearer together than at the start (handles roughly shoulder-width or slightly closer) without clanking. Palms still face forward, wrists still neutral and stacked directly over the elbows so the forearm-to-hand line is straight. Scapulae still depressed and retracted; shoulders not jammed up into the ears. Torso unchanged: head, shoulders and glutes still touching the bench, lower back NOT arched off the pad, ribcage down, feet still flat on the floor. Gaze still straight ahead, chin level - the head does not poke forward under the weight. Lowering reverses the path by flexing the elbows, actively contracting the lats to pull the dumbbells back down to shoulder level in control, so the animated frames show the elbows tracking down and slightly forward until the upper arms are just below shoulder height.
exercises.hand_grip_detail: Closed, pronated grip - palms facing forward with the thumbs wrapped around the handles. Hands at shoulder-width or slightly wider, each dumbbell centred in the palm so the handle crosses the base of the fingers and the weight stacks over the forearm bones. Wrists held in a neutral position with no flexion or extension, so that at every point of the rep the handle sits directly above the wrist, elbow and shoulder; the knuckles point up at the top of the press. Pinkies and elbows stay pointed mostly forward through the press rather than straight out to the side.
exercises.body_alignment_cues: Three points of contact at the bench - head, shoulders and glutes - held for every rep, with the feet flat on the floor as the base. Core braced to keep the ribcage over the pelvis and stop the lumbar spine arching as the arms go overhead. Scapulae retracted and depressed throughout. The elbows are the key visual: they stay pointed in front of the body rather than flaring into a goal-post, which keeps the humeral head moving cleanly in the socket. Shoulder and elbow are the animated joints; spine, hips, knees and ankles are a held pose. On the standing version, feet are hip-width, knees slightly bent and the core locks the ribcage down so no backward lean or hip thrust appears.
common_form_mistakes: Arching the lower back and leaning back so the press becomes an incline press - the lumbar spine lifting off the bench pad
Flaring the elbows straight out to the sides into a 'goal post' position, which compresses the shoulder joint and is linked to rotator cuff problems
Letting the head, upper back or glutes lose contact with the bench, or lifting the feet off the floor
Breaking the wrists back so the dumbbells sit behind the forearm line instead of stacked over the wrist and elbow
Pressing the dumbbells forward in front of the face instead of up over the shoulders
Shrugging the shoulders up into the ears and losing scapular depression
Dropping the dumbbells on the eccentric instead of pulling them down with the lats under control
Pressing the arms up out of sync (one side leading) or clanging the dumbbells together at the top
Pushing the chin/head forward under the load
Going too heavy without a spotter positioned behind with hands near the wrists

exercises.name: Walking Lunge (dumbbells optional)
exercises.equipment: Bodyweight, or one dumbbell in each hand; needs clear floor space to travel
exercises.primary_muscles: Gluteus maximus and quadriceps of the front leg (primary); hamstrings and adductors assist; hip flexors and quads of the trailing leg, plus calves, core and hip abductors for balance
exercises.start_position: Standing tall with feet hip-width apart, toes pointing straight forward, weight even through both feet. A dumbbell in each hand, palms facing each other (neutral grip), arms straight down by the sides so the dumbbells hang beside the outer thighs. Back straight, spine neutral, chest lifted, shoulders down and back, abdominals tight. Head in line with the spine, chin level, gaze straight ahead at a fixed point on the horizon (not down at the feet) for balance. Then a long step forward with the lead leg - roughly one full stride, about 60-90 cm depending on height - landing with the lead foot flat, toes pointing straight ahead, directly in line with the hip (not crossed toward the midline, not turned out). At the moment of landing the body is in a split stance: lead shin near vertical, trailing leg extended behind with the heel lifted and the weight on the ball of the trailing foot, both feet roughly hip-width apart side to side, torso still vertical.
exercises.end_position: Bottom of the lunge: hips lowered straight down so both knees are bent to about 90 degrees. The front thigh is roughly parallel with the floor, the front shin near vertical, and the front knee sits directly above the ankle - stacked over the heel/mid-foot, NOT pushed out past the toes - and tracking in line over the second and third toes with no inward collapse. The trailing knee hovers about 2-10 cm above the floor, directly under or slightly behind the trailing hip, with that shin angled back and the rear heel lifted so the toes are tucked under and the ball of the foot is loaded. Torso stays upright and vertical, perpendicular to the floor, with its natural lumbar curve, chest lifted, abdominals tight and hips square to the direction of travel (no twist, no side tilt). Arms still hanging straight down with the dumbbells beside the front and rear thighs, shoulders down. Head neutral, gaze still forward at the fixed horizon point. To finish the rep the front foot drives into the ground and the hips extend until both knees straighten; the trailing leg then swings through to become the new lead leg, stepping forward into the next lunge (or, in the stationary version, both feet come back together at the starting stance). An animation of this needs at least four keyframes: tall stance, step-and-touchdown, 90/90 bottom, and drive-up with the rear leg swinging through - plus a visible alternation of lead leg between reps.
exercises.hand_grip_detail: One dumbbell per hand, closed neutral grip - thumbs wrapped around the handles, palms facing in toward the thighs. Handles centred in the palm, arms straight down by the sides with the elbows extended and relaxed, dumbbells about 5-10 cm clear of the outer thighs so they do not bang the leg during the step-through. Bodyweight version: hands lightly on the hips, folded at the chest, or held out for balance. Loaded front-rack variation: elbows bent about 90 degrees and tucked into the sides of the abdominals with the dumbbells at chest height.
exercises.body_alignment_cues: Torso upright and erect through the whole stride, abdominals engaged, chest lifted, shoulders and shoulder blades down - the solution to a balance or strength shortfall is never to lean forward. Spine neutral; hips level and square (no hip drop on the swing-leg side, no rotation). The movement is a vertical drop of the hips between the two feet, not a forward dive over the front knee. Front knee stacked over the ankle and tracking over the toes; even a slight inward turn of the lead foot or lead knee raises torque stress at that knee. Rear heel stays up with the ankle dorsiflexed and the toes tucked. Gaze fixed on the horizon to stabilize the head and the whole chain.
common_form_mistakes: Leaning the torso too far forward on the way down, which increases shear force at the knee joint and injury risk (the most common beginner error per NSCA)
Letting the front knee travel out past the toes instead of staying above the ankle
Front knee or lead foot turning inward (valgus collapse), which raises torque stress on the front knee
Taking too short a step, which jams the front knee forward and leaves the rear knee under-bent
Slamming the trailing knee into the floor instead of stopping just above it
Pushing off the rear leg to stand up instead of driving through the front foot
Letting the hips rotate, tilt or drop to the side - losing square hips
Looking down at the feet, which pulls the chest and spine forward
Arching the lower back or letting the ribcage flare as the hips drop
Landing with the feet on a narrow tightrope line rather than hip-width apart, destroying the balance base
Bouncing out of the bottom without control, or letting the dumbbells swing and pull the torso off balance

exercises.name: Leg Press (seated machine)
exercises.equipment: Seated/selectorized leg press machine with an adjustable seat and a resistance plate
exercises.primary_muscles: Gluteus maximus, quadriceps and hamstrings (primary); adductors and calves assist; abdominals brace the spine
exercises.start_position: Seated in the machine with the back and sacrum (tailbone) flat against the backrest - the whole lumbar and pelvic region in contact with the pad, with no gap behind the lower back and no rounding. Feet placed flat on the resistance plate with the toes pointing forward, feet about hip- to shoulder-width apart and symmetrical on the plate, heels in full contact. Seat and foot position adjusted so the knees are bent to approximately 90 degrees at the start, with the knees tracking in line over the feet (shins angled, thighs close to the plate line). Hands lightly grasping the machine handles beside the seat to stabilize the upper body - a light hold, not a yank. Abdominals braced to stabilize the spine. Shoulders back against the pad, head resting in line with the spine against the headrest or backrest, chin level, gaze straight ahead along the line of the press (not tucked down to the chest, not twisted to a mirror).
exercises.end_position: Hips and knees extended so the resistance plate is pushed away to a comfortable, relaxed near-straight position - knees close to, but short of, full extension (roughly 160-175 degrees) and deliberately NOT hyperextended or locked out. Legs form a near-straight line from hip through knee to ankle, with the knees still tracking directly over the feet and no inward or outward drift. Heels stay flat and pressed against the plate - no heel lift onto the toes. Back and sacrum still flat against the backrest with the lower back unmoved; the hips do not lift off or slide up the seat. Hands still lightly on the handles, shoulders down, head neutral, gaze forward. Return by slowly flexing the hips and knees, letting the plate travel back in control until the knees are bent about 90 degrees again - stopping before the upper thighs compress the ribcage or the pelvis tucks under and the lumbar spine rounds off the pad. Both the press and the return are animated at a controlled tempo; only hips, knees and ankles move while the trunk is a held pose.
exercises.hand_grip_detail: Not a grip-driven lift: both hands rest lightly on the machine's side handles (or the edges of the seat pad) with the fingers wrapped and the thumbs around, elbows slightly bent and relaxed, upper arms by the sides. The handles exist to stabilize the upper body and keep the torso pinned to the backrest - the grip stays loose enough that the arms are not pulling the chest forward or helping to shift load.
exercises.body_alignment_cues: Back and sacrum flat on the backrest throughout - the single most important alignment point; abdominals braced so the low back does not move in either direction. Hips stay seated, glutes down. Knees track in line with the feet and the hips, never collapsing inward. Heels stay flat on the plate as the anchor of the push. No upper-body movement: no head lift, no neck push into the pad, no twisting. Depth is limited by whatever point the pelvis stays neutral - the thighs must never compress the ribcage. Hips, knees and ankles are the only animated joints.
common_form_mistakes: Hyperextending or locking out the knees at the top of the press
Letting the hips/buttocks lift off the seat or the lower back round off the pad as the plate comes back in
Going too deep so the upper thighs compress the ribcage and the pelvis tucks under
Lifting the heels off the plate and pressing through the toes
Knees collapsing inward (valgus) under load instead of tracking over the feet
Setting the feet too high, too low or asymmetrically on the plate so the start knee angle is far from 90 degrees
Pulling on the handles or pushing the head back into the pad to drive the weight
Bouncing the plate out of the bottom position rather than controlling both the press and the return
Holding the breath / failing to brace, letting the spine move with each rep
Letting the plate crash back in on the return

exercises.name: Front Plank (forearm plank)
exercises.primary_muscles: Rectus abdominis, transverse abdominis and obliques (anterior core); erector spinae and the deep back stabilizers; quadriceps, glutes, serratus anterior and shoulder stabilizers hold the frame
exercises.start_position: Begin lying prone (face down) on a mat. Elbows tucked close to the sides of the ribs and placed directly under the shoulders, forearms flat on the floor and roughly parallel to each other (or hands lightly clasped), palms down and hands facing forward. Legs extended straight behind, feet about hip-width or closer with the ankles dorsiflexed - toes pulled toward the shins so the toe pads are planted and the heels point up at the ceiling. Quadriceps contracted to lock the knees straight. Core and abdominal muscles contracted to stiffen the torso into one rigid unit before any lift happens. Head in line with the spine, neck long, gaze down at the floor just in front of the hands.
exercises.end_position: The whole torso, hips and legs lifted off the floor and held as one straight, stiff line from the crown of the head through the shoulders, hips, knees and ankles - the only contact points are the forearms/hands and the toes. Shoulders stacked directly over the elbows, upper arms close to vertical, elbows still at about 90 degrees and still tucked near the ribs, palms flat and facing down. Shoulder blades set flat on the ribcage - no shrug up toward the ears and no collapse between the shoulder blades. Pelvis neutral: no sag or arch in the lower back, and no hiking of the hips up into a tent. Glutes and quads engaged, knees fully straight, ankles still dorsiflexed with the weight on the toe pads. Head neutral and in line with the spine, gaze down and slightly forward at the floor, chin neither tucked to the chest nor craned up. Breathing continues normally while the position is held for at least five seconds and up to the target time; the exercise is then finished by lowering back to the floor with the torso still rigid and the legs still extended. For animation, the moving frames are the lift-off and the controlled lower - the hold itself animates only through breathing and the small postural corrections, so sagging hips or a rising pelvis should read as the error states, not the motion.
exercises.hand_grip_detail: No implement to grip. Palms flat on the floor, hands facing forward (fingers pointing ahead), spread with light even pressure through the whole palm and the forearms pressing down into the mat. Elbows directly beneath the shoulder joints and drawn in close to the sides of the body, forearms about shoulder-width apart - not splayed out wide and not crossed in front. In the clasped-hand version the fingers interlace with the forearms still parallel-ish and the elbows still under the shoulders; in a high plank the same stacking applies, with the wrists directly under the shoulders and the fingers spread forward.
exercises.body_alignment_cues: One rigid line: head, shoulders, hips, knees and ankles in a single plane. Abdominals and core contracted to stiffen the torso; glutes and quads switched on to keep the hips level and the knees locked. Shoulders directly over the elbows with the shoulder blades flat and the neck long - no shrug. Ankles dorsiflexed, toes pulled toward the shins. Nothing should move once the position is set; the body is held as one piece rather than hinged at the hips. Keep breathing throughout rather than holding the breath.
common_form_mistakes: Sagging or arching in the lower back so the hips drop toward the floor
Hiking the hips upward into a pike/tent to take load off the core
Bending the knees instead of keeping the legs fully extended
Shrugging the shoulders up toward the ears and losing the flat shoulder-blade position
Letting the elbows drift forward of or behind the shoulders instead of staying stacked directly underneath
Flaring the elbows wide away from the sides of the ribs
Dropping the head or craning it up instead of keeping it in line with the spine
Holding the breath - breathing must continue through the hold
Holding the position past the point where form breaks down (stop when the line is lost rather than chasing time)
Continuing through lower-back pain instead of stopping and seeking medical advice

exercises.name: Lat Pulldown (seated, to the front)
exercises.equipment: Seated lat pulldown machine (selectorized) with an adjustable thigh pad and a long bar attachment
exercises.primary_muscles: Latissimus dorsi (primary); teres major, rhomboids, mid and lower trapezius, posterior deltoid and biceps brachii/brachialis assist; abdominals brace the spine
exercises.start_position: Seated in the machine with the lower body anchored - the thigh pad adjusted so it sits firmly against the top of the thighs, feet flat on the floor about hip-width apart and the knees bent to roughly 90 degrees. Abdominals braced ('stiffened') to stabilize the spine, with the natural lumbar curve kept and no arching of the low back. Reach up overhead to grasp the bar firmly with both hands, in an overhand (pronated) grip set a little wider than shoulder-width so that, once the bar is pulled down, the forearms end up near vertical. With the arms extended overhead (elbows nearly straight, about 170-180 degrees, upper arms framing the head), depress and retract the scapulae - pull the shoulders down and back out of the shrugged position - and hold that set. The torso leans back slightly from vertical, no more than about 30 degrees, with the legs providing support; the chest is lifted toward the bar and the spine stays long. Head aligned with the spine, chin level, gaze up and forward at the bar or just above the horizon.
exercises.end_position: Bar pulled down in front of the face to the top or mid-section of the chest - finishing roughly at collarbone-to-upper-sternum height, a few centimetres from the chest. Elbows driven directly downward toward the floor and in toward the sides of the torso, finishing at about 45-70 degrees of flexion with the upper arms down alongside the ribs and the forearms close to vertical and in line with the cable. Scapulae fully depressed and retracted - the shoulder blades pulled down and together so the chest is open and the shoulders are nowhere near the ears. Wrists straight and in line with the forearms, grip still overhand. Torso lean unchanged from the start - still at that same slight backward lean, with no extra rocking back during the pull - thighs still pinned under the pad, feet still flat, lumbar spine not arched. Head still in line with the spine, gaze up/forward at the bar. The pull stops the moment the elbows stop travelling downward and begin to travel backward; pulling any further loads the shoulder joint. Pause briefly, then reverse: the bar rises in control as the elbows extend back to full extension overhead, and only then do the scapulae rise slightly to full stretch. Animation keyframes: arms overhead with scapulae set, scapular depression initiating the pull, elbows driving down to the chest-level finish, then the controlled return.
exercises.hand_grip_detail: Both hands grip the bar firmly, overhand/pronated with the palms facing away and the thumbs wrapped around the bar opposite the fingers. Hands set symmetrically about the body's midline, roughly 1.3 to 1.5 times shoulder-width apart (just outside the shoulders) - wide enough that the forearms finish vertical at chest level but not so wide that the elbows cannot drive down. The bar sits across the base of the fingers into the palm, with the wrists held straight and neutral, never curled or hooked back over the bar. The elbows point down and slightly out at the top and pull in toward the ribs at the bottom. (A neutral or supinated close grip is a legitimate variation but changes the arm path: elbows stay closer to the body throughout.)
exercises.body_alignment_cues: Lower body anchored by the thigh pad with the feet flat - no lifting out of the seat. Abdominals braced and the low back kept out of extension; the only torso position is that single slight backward lean (no more than about 30 degrees) which is set before the pull and held, not added to during it. Scapulae depressed and retracted as the start of every rep and held throughout - the pull is INITIATED by depressing the shoulder blades and only then by bending the elbows. Elbows are the thing to watch: they drive straight down toward the floor and in toward the torso, and the rep ends when they stop going down and start going back. Head stays in line with the spine. Hips, knees and feet are a held pose; shoulders and elbows are the animated joints.
common_form_mistakes: Rocking the torso backward during the pull to heave the bar down, adding lean beyond the set position
Leaning back more than about 30 degrees, which turns the pulldown into a row
Pulling the bar past the chest so the elbows travel backward instead of downward, which puts extra stress into the shoulder joint
Arching the lower back / losing the abdominal brace as the bar comes down
Starting the pull with the arms (elbow flexion) instead of initiating with scapular depression - letting the biceps lead
Letting the shoulders shrug up into the ears at the top and never resetting scapular depression
Pulling the bar behind the neck rather than to the front of the chest
Letting the bar yank the arms up at the end of the rep and the body lift out of the seat, instead of controlling the return and only then letting the scapulae rise slightly
Setting the thigh pad too loose so the hips rise on every rep
Breaking the wrists over the bar instead of keeping them straight
Grip so wide that the elbows cannot drive down and the range collapses
